statement: Thirty lanterns hang in a circle, numbered $0$ to $29$. A spark starts at lantern $0$, and every second it moves $8$ places clockwise and lights the lantern it lands on, so its first jump takes it from lantern $0$ to lantern $8$. Lantern $0$ is lit at the start. How many different lanterns are ever lit?

choices.misconception: I counted the 15 lanterns and then counted lantern 0 a second time when the spark came back to it.
I thought the spark would land on every lantern sooner or later, but it only ever lands on even-numbered lanterns.
I found the least common multiple of 8 and 30, which is 120, and gave that, but 120 is how many lanterns the spark passes before it is back at 0, not how many it lights.
I multiplied 8 by 30 to find when the spark gets back to lantern 0, and gave 240 as the answer.

hints: After $k$ jumps the spark is at lantern $8k$, minus as many $30$s as needed to get a number from $0$ to $29$.
Since $8$ and $30$ are both even, the spark only lands on even-numbered lanterns. Does it reach all of them before returning to $0$?
The spark is back at lantern $0$ when $8k$ is a multiple of $30$. The first time is $k = 15$.

solutions.reliable: After $k$ jumps the spark is at the remainder of $8k$ when divided by $30$. It is back at lantern $0$ when $30$ divides $8k$, that is, when $15$ divides $4k$, which first happens at $k = 15$. The positions for $k = 0, 1, \ldots, 14$ are all different, because if $8i$ and $8j$ left the same remainder, $30$ would divide $8(i - j)$ and $15$ would divide $i - j$. After that the pattern repeats. So exactly $15$ lanterns are lit: all the even-numbered ones, $0, 8, 16, 24, 2, 10, \ldots$.
solutions.elegant: The spark always lands on even-numbered lanterns, and there are $30 / \gcd(8, 30) = 15$ different stops before the pattern repeats, so it lights all $15$ even-numbered lanterns.
